item.title: jyotirmaTha lineage
item.description:
The Jyotirmaṭha Śaṅkarācārya Lineage in the 20th Century
Vidyāśaṅkar Sundareśan

This page was first born in response to the INDOLOGY listserv discussion (January 19, 1998) about the [Śaṅkarācārya of the North], and has been updated a few times since then. Barring fresh developments in future, this version (July 2000) will be final.

There is currently a succession dispute at the Jyotirmaṭha Śaṅkarācārya seat, the origin of which dates back to the year 1953. Till recently, the two major rivals were Svāmī Svarūpānanda Sarasvatī (who is also the Śaṅkarācārya of Dvārakā in the west) and Svāmī Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī. Since 1993-4, another Saṃnyāsin named Mādhava Āśrama has been a third claimant to the Jyotirmaṭha title.

item.title: kAnchI-maTha-history 94
item.description:
Subject: Real history of the Kanchi math (Re: Former President Inaugurates…) Celebrations
From: vidya@cco.caltech.edu (Vidyasankar Sundaresan)
Date: 3 Aug 1994 04:05:16 GMT

Both this post and a previous one by Bon Giovanni have raised questions of historicity of Adi Sankaracharya and the Kanchi math. This is not a new question. It is generally accepted as tradition that Adi Sankaracharya, the famous Advaita philosopher, founded four maths (monasteries) at Sringeri, Puri, Dwaraka and Badrinath; that he ascended the famous sarvagna-pitha in Kashmir, and finally passed away near Kedarnath. None of the four recognized mathas claims jurisdiction over the other three. However, the Kanchi math claims that Sankaracharya established a fifth math in Kanchi, with jurisdiction over the recognized four mathas; that Sankaracharya ascended a sarvagna-pitha not in Kashmir, but at Kanchi, and that he passed away not in Kedarnath, but at Kanchi. These and other such claims have been widely publicized by the followers of the Kanchi math with the direct participation of and encouragement from the heads of the Kanchi math, including the recently departed centenarian Sri Chandrasekharendra Saraswati (C.S., for short) and his successor Sri Jayendra Saraswati (J.S.).

item.title: Shaṅkaravijaya History
item.description:
Conflicting hagiographies and history: The place of Śaṅkaravijaya texts in Advaita tradition
Vidyasankar Sundaresan

Gemini summary - dates

Based on the provided text, here is a table of the determined date ranges for the various texts considered:

Text Author/Attribution Determined Date/Range
Śaṅkara’s undisputed works Śaṅkarācārya Early 8th Century CE
Madhavīya Śaṅkaravijaya (or Samksepa Śaṅkarajaya) Traditionally Vidyāraṇya Composed before 1783 CE, with traditional attribution placing it in the 14th Century CE.
Anantānandagiri’s Śaṅkaravijaya Anantānandagiri Post-14th Century CE
Cidvilāsa’s Śaṅkaravijaya Vilāsa Cidvilāsa Possibly 17th Century CE or later
Sadānanda’s Śaṅkaravijaya Sāra Sadānanda 1783 CE
Rājacūḍāmaṇi dīkṣita’s Śaṅkarābhyudaya Rājacūḍāmaṇi dīkṣita 17th Century CE
Govindanātha’s Śaṅkarācāryacarita (Keralīya Śaṅkaravijaya) Govindanātha Usually dated to the 17th Century CE
Br̥hat Śaṅkaravijaya Attributed to Citsukha Existence is uncertain; Citsukha is identified as a 13th-century author.
Prācīna Śaṅkaravijaya Attributed to Anandagiri Existence is uncertain; Anandagiri, the commentator, lived in the 13th Century CE.
Naiṣadhīyacarita Śrīharṣa 12th Century CE
Vyāsācala’s Śaṅkaravijaya Vyāsācala One scholar dates it to the 15th Century CE.
Tirumala Dīkṣita’s Śaṅkarābhyudaya Tirumala Dīkṣita Around 1700 CE
Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita’s Patañjalicarita Rāmabhadra dīkṣita 17th Century CE
Vedāntakalpataru Amalānanda Early 13th Century CE
Ḍiṇḍima (Commentary on Mādhavīya) Dhanapatisūrin Completed in 1798 CE
Advaitarājyalakṣmi (Commentary on Mādhavīya) Acyutarāya 1824 CE
Śrī Gurucaritra Gangādhara Sarasvatī 15th Century CE Marathi text
Nilakantha’s works, Hosinga Vāsudeva dīkṣita’s work, Lakṣmaṇasūrin’s work Various Described as being “about a century old” at the time the paper was written.
Gemini - disputes

Anantānandagiri’s Śaṅkaravijaya (or Anandagirīya)

  • Authorship and Dating Dispute: The work is frequently misattributed to the 13th-century commentator Anandagiri. The text itself proves this is false, as it quotes from a 14th-century work (Adhikaraṇa Ratnamālā). The author’s name is Anantānandagiri, and his claim of being a direct disciple of Śaṅkara is anachronistic.
  • Contradictory Editions (Calcutta vs. 1971 Madras):
    • Śaṅkara’s Birthplace: The 19th-century Calcutta editions state Śaṅkara was born in Cidambaram. The 1971 Madras edition, edited by N. Veezhinathan, changes this to Kālaṭi, claiming the Cidambaram version is a falsehood.
    • Maṭha Establishments: The Calcutta editions mention the establishment of a maṭha only at Śr̥ṅgeri, with Sureśvara as its head. The 1971 edition claims a maṭha was established near Śr̥ṅgeri with Padmapāda as its head and reserves Sureśvara for a newly mentioned maṭha at Kāñcīpuram.
  • Interpolated/Altered Passages in the 1971 Edition:
    • A phrase reading “having established the lineage at Śr̥ṅgeri” in older manuscripts is changed to “having established the lineage at Kāñcī and other cities.”
    • Veiled references to the Vaiṣṇava teachers Rāmānuja and Mādhva (portrayed as disciples of Śaṅkara) are put in parentheses, with the editor claiming they are “late interpolations.”
    • Details about a yogaliṅga at Kāñcīpuram are added, citing the unavailable Mārkaṇḍeya Saṁhitā.
  • Dispute over Mahāvākyas: The 1971 edition parenthetically adds a fifth mahāvākya (’neha nānāsti kiṁcana’), while a footnote argues for ‘om tat sat’. This contradicts the original text’s own reference to the “four great sentences” (mahāvākya-catuṣṭaya).
  • Overall Credibility: Śr̥ṅgeri followers have consistently rejected the text as a forgery. Scholar A.C. Burnell described it in 1880 as a “modern and unreliable text written in the interests of the schismatic maṭhas.” The analysis in the provided document concludes that the 1971 edition is “nothing more than a faithful reproduction of the Kāñcī maṭha’s latest version of this text.”

Madhavīya Śaṅkaravijaya (or Samksepa Śaṅkarajaya)

  • Authorship Dispute: The central controversy is its authorship. It is traditionally attributed to the 14th-century sage Vidyāraṇya. Kāñcī maṭha followers dispute this, claiming it is a late 19th-century work by one Bhaṭṭaśrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī. The existence of a 1798 CE commentary disproves the 19th-century theory.
  • Allegations of Plagiarism: Kāñcī maṭha claims the Mādhavīya is a plagiarized work that borrows heavily from other texts, primarily Vyāsācala’s Śaṅkaravijaya and the works of Tirumala Dīkṣita and Rājacūḍāmaṇi Dīkṣita. Śr̥ṅgeri followers argue the borrowing was in the opposite direction.
  • Allegations of Tampering: It is claimed that the text was significantly altered in the late 19th century to enhance the importance of Śr̥ṅgeri over Kāñcī. The provided text’s author states this charge is “disproved by evidence to the contrary,” as all manuscripts and printed editions are remarkably consistent.
  • Disputed Verses: Two verses referring to a poet named Vyāsācala are found in a single Madras manuscript but are absent from all other manuscripts and printed editions. Their authenticity is highly suspect.

Br̥hat Śaṅkaravijaya and Prācīna Śaṅkaravijaya

  • Dispute over Existence: The primary dispute is whether these texts ever actually existed. No independent scholar has located any manuscripts.
  • Unverified Claims: The only source claiming their existence and quoting from them are publications from the Kāñcī maṭha, which the provided text describes as unreliable.
  • Conflicting Attributions: The Prācīna Śaṅkaravijaya is attributed to Anandagiri by one source and to the 15th-century poet Mūkakavi by another, both via Kāñcī maṭha sources.

Vyāsācala’s Śaṅkaravijaya

  • Authorship Dispute: The author’s identity is unknown, with Kāñcī maṭha sources providing conflicting identifications over time. The analysis suggests “Vyāsācala” may not be an independent author but another name for Mādhava (author of the Mādhavīya).
  • Interpolated Verses: The 1954 printed edition includes a postscript with four additional verses describing Śaṅkara establishing a maṭha and spending his last days at Kāñcī. The editor explicitly states these verses were not found in any of his source manuscripts and were supplied separately by a Kāñcī maṭha paṇḍita.

Naiṣadhīyacarita by Śrīharṣa

  • Deliberate Textual Tampering: The Kāñcī maṭha cites a verse from this 12th-century poem as early proof of its yogaliṅga. To do so, the word yāgeśvaraḥ (lord of sacrifices) in the original text is changed to yogeśvaraḥ (lord of yoga). All known manuscripts and commentaries support the original yāgeśvaraḥ reading, making this a clear case of textual manipulation.

Govindanātha’s Śaṅkarācāryacarita (Keralīya Śaṅkaravijaya)

  • Interpolated Verses: Kāñcī maṭha sources claim the existence of six additional verses stating that Śaṅkara established a maṭha at Kāñcī and died there. These verses are not found in any known manuscript and directly contradict the text’s own narrative that Śaṅkara passed away in Trichūr.

Rājacūḍāmaṇi Dīkṣita’s Śaṅkarābhyudaya

  • Disputed Chapters: The most complete manuscript (from the Adyar Library) contains six chapters. The published edition contains eight chapters, with the final two (which mention a Sarvajñapīṭha at Kāñcīpuram) being sourced from a Kāñcī maṭha manuscript, raising questions about their authenticity as part of the original work.

Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita’s Patañjalicarita

  • Disputed Chapter: The final chapter, which is the only part that mentions Śaṅkara, is considered a possible later addition as it “does not naturally fit in with the preceding chapters” of the poem about the grammarian Patañjali.

Pañcīkaraṇa

  • Dispute over Content (Misrepresentation): A scholar aligned with the Kāñcī maṭha claimed the text lists only three mahāvākyas (great sentences) to undermine the standard tradition of four. The provided analysis refutes this by quoting the text, which explicitly lists four sentences, showing the claim to be a misrepresentation.
